title: Tile Boxes Coverage Calculator — How Many Boxes Do I Need? | Hacé Cuentas
description: Calculate exactly how many tile boxes you need for any room. Enter area in m², coverage per box, and waste percentage — get boxes needed instantly. Free, no signup.
intro: Planning a tiling job? Enter your total area in m², the coverage per box (printed on the packaging), and your expected waste factor. The calculator applies the standard formula — **Boxes = ceil(area × (1 + waste%) / m² per box)** — and rounds up to the nearest whole box so you never run short. Standard waste is 10% for straight-lay; increase to 15% for diagonal, 18% for herringbone patterns.
keyTakeaway: Formula: **Boxes = ⌈ Area m² × (1 + Waste%) / m²-per-box ⌉**. Always round UP — you cannot buy half a box. Standard waste factor is **10%** for straight-lay; go to **15–20%** for diagonal or complex cuts.

Estimating floor tiles for a kitchen or living room with doorway cut-outs.
Quoting material quantities before visiting the tile store or placing an online order.
Checking whether the tiles already in your cart are enough before checkout.

explanation:
## How it works

The standard industry formula for tile quantity estimation is:

**Boxes = ⌈ Area × (1 + Waste / 100) / Coverage-per-box ⌉**

Where ⌈ ⌉ means ceiling (round up to the next whole number), because you always buy full boxes.

### Step-by-step

1. **Measure your area** — length × width for floors; perimeter × height for walls. Deduct large openings (door ~1.6 m², window ~1 m²) but ignore small obstacles under 0.5 m².
2. **Choose your waste factor** — 10% for straight lay, 15% for 45° diagonal, 18% for herringbone/chevron, 20% for complex mosaic patterns.
3. **Find m² per box** — it is printed on the packaging. If not, calculate: tile length (m) × tile width (m) × tiles per box.
4. **Apply the formula** and round up.

### Common tile sizes and coverage per box

| Tile size (cm) | Tiles/box | m²/box | Typical use |
|---|---|---|---|
| 20×20 | 25 | 1.00 | Bathroom walls, skirting |
| 20×30 | 17 | 1.02 | Wall tiles |
| 30×30 | 11 | 0.99 | Bathroom floor |
| 30×60 | 8 | 1.44 | Modern wall tiles |
| 45×45 | 6 | 1.22 | Living room floor |
| 60×60 | 4 | 1.44 | Porcelain floor |
| 60×120 | 2 | 1.44 | Large-format porcelain |

### Waste factors by installation type

| Layout | Waste to add |
|---|---|
| Straight / brick bond | 10% |
| Diagonal (45°) | 15% |
| Herringbone / chevron | 18% |
| Mosaic or complex pattern | 20% |
| Large-format (≥60×60 cm) | 12–15% |

## Common mistakes

1. **Buying from different production lots** — tiles vary subtly in shade between batches. Buy all boxes at once and verify the lot number on each box.
2. **Forgetting the waste factor** — running out mid-project risks a lot mismatch if you reorder.
3. **Deducting small obstacles** — do not subtract openings under 0.5 m²; those cuts generate waste anyway.
4. **Not keeping a spare box** — buy 1 extra box for future repairs. Discontinued models are impossible to match later.

faq.q: How do I find the m² coverage per box if it's not on the packaging?
faq.a: Calculate it yourself: tile length (m) × tile width (m) × number of tiles per box. For 30×60 cm tiles in a box of 8: 0.30 × 0.60 × 8 = **1.44 m²**. For 45×45 cm tiles, box of 6: 0.45 × 0.45 × 6 = **1.215 m²**. Most packaging does list this value.

faq.q: Should I use 10% or 15% waste for my project?
faq.a: Use **10%** for standard straight-lay patterns in rectangular rooms. Use **15%** for tiles installed at 45° diagonal or for large-format tiles (60×60 cm or larger) where edge cuts waste more material. Use **18–20%** for herringbone, chevron, or complex mosaic layouts with many angles.

faq.q: Why do I always need to round up to the nearest whole box?
faq.a: Tile stores sell complete boxes — you cannot buy 9.17 boxes. Rounding down means you run short before finishing. Rounding up gives you a small surplus from the same production lot, which you can use for future repairs or return if the store allows it.

faq.q: What is the formula for wall tiles in a bathroom?
faq.a: Measure each wall individually: width × height. Sum all walls, then subtract large openings (doors ~1.6 m², windows ~1 m²). For a 2×3 m bathroom with 2.4 m ceilings: (2+3)×2 × 2.4 = 24 m² gross, minus 1.6 m² door and 1 m² window = **21.4 m²**. Enter 21.4 into the calculator.

faq.q: How do I calculate tiles for both floor and walls?
faq.a: Run the calculator twice — once for the floor area and once for the total wall area, since floors and walls often use different tile sizes and may have different waste factors. Add the two box totals together for your final shopping list.

faq.q: What happens if I run out of tiles mid-project?
faq.a: You risk a shade mismatch. Tiles are made in production lots (batches), and the same model from a different batch can have a slightly different color. Always buy all boxes at once from the same lot, and ask the store to hold extra boxes if needed.

faq.q: Can I use this calculator for outdoor tiles and patios?
faq.a: Yes. The area-to-boxes formula is the same regardless of the application — indoor floor, wall, outdoor terrace, or swimming pool surround. For outdoors, choose tiles rated for outdoor use (frost-resistant for cold climates) and consider a slightly higher waste factor (12–15%) for more complex perimeters.

faq.q: Can I return unused boxes to the store?
faq.a: Most large hardware chains accept returns of **sealed, unopened boxes** within 30 days with a receipt. Once opened, returns are typically not accepted. However, it is wise to keep 1 sealed spare box for future repairs — tile models are discontinued frequently and later reorders may not match.

faq.q: Is the 10% waste factor always enough?
faq.a: For simple rectangular rooms with straight-lay patterns, yes. In rooms with many cut-outs (toilets, bathtubs, pipes), unusual shapes, or decorative border tiles, bump the waste to 12–15%. Commercial installers sometimes quote 15% as their standard to cover all scenarios safely.
